\begin{proof}
Let $s = \operatorname{nim}(2,b_1,\dots,b_m)=2\oplus(b_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_m)$.
Every position in this family is winning, since $s\in\{2,3\}$; hence strong mastery requires a winning move on every input in the reduction.
The most significant bit of $s$ is $2$ (the $2^1$ bit), and among the heaps only the first heap has that bit set. Therefore, any move that makes the nim-sum zero must change the first heap.
The unique choice that makes the new nim-sum zero is
\[
x_1' \;=\; 2 \oplus s \;=\; b_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_m \in \{0,1\},
\]
so the winning move is uniquely determined by the parity of $(b_1,\dots,b_m)$.

Use two bits per heap: the encoding fixes the first heap to $10$ and maps each input bit $b_i$ to the heap $0b_i$, using only constants and wiring. The least significant bit of the selected replacement for the first heap is then the input parity. Thus both encoding and decoding preserve polynomial size and constant depth, with Boolean input length $n=2(m+1)$. This is a reduction to winning-move selection even though all encoded positions have the same win/loss classification.
\end{proof}
